title: Token Minting
summary:
To **mint** is to create something new under authority that others can recognise as genuine, usually with an expiry. Only the mint strikes coins; anyone can tell a real one. In systems: **issuer signs, verifier checks, TTL or revoke.**

Ask three questions of any mint (a good interview template):
1. **Who may mint?** The issuer holds the signing secret. Long-lived secrets stay home; the outside world receives only short-lived, narrow things.
2. **How does a verifier check?** By signature alone (stateless, no database hit) or by lookup (stateful).
3. **How does it expire or get revoked?** TTL, refresh, denylist, key rotation.

A signed payload is trusted if the signature verifies, so you can hand an otherwise untrusted object to a stranger: pre-signed S3 URLs, JWT access tokens (`sub`, `scope`, `exp`), reset and verification links, CDN signed URLs, webhook signatures, job tokens (`job_id`, `attempt`, `lease_expiry`).

Signing is not encryption: anyone can read a JWT payload. Put in claims fixed at issue time and fine to be stale until expiry (user id, scopes), never secrets.

Verification options: HMAC with a shared secret (every verifier could also mint) or asymmetric keys (private signs, public verifies; publish and rotate with key ids).

Revocation is the cost of statelessness: a bearer token is valid until `exp` unless a denylist is checked, so keep TTLs short and refresh.

Minting is broader than tokens: keys and certs (a KMS data key wrapped by a master key), unique IDs (Snowflake), and coordination numbers ([fencing token](#/sd/f/fencing-token), [lease](#/sd/f/lease), epochs) where higher wins. See [IdP](#/sd/f/idp).

drills.q: A KMS call `GenerateDataKey` returns a plaintext data key and the same key encrypted under a master key. The application encrypts data with the plaintext key, stores the encrypted key beside the data and discards the plaintext. Which minting principle is this?
options: Fencing: the higher key number wins
The master key never leaves the issuer; it mints small one-off keys that do the work, and only the issuer can unwrap them later
drills.explain: The long-lived secret stays in the issuer (KMS). The minted artefact is narrow and short-lived in memory. It is the same shape as a JWT signer and its tokens.

drills.q: Which claims suit a JWT access token that verifiers check only by signature? Select all that apply.
drills.explain: Claims should be fixed at issue time and acceptable if stale until `exp`. The payload is readable by anyone who holds the token, so no secrets, and a fast-changing value like a balance would be wrong the moment it changes.

drills.q: A service verifies JWTs locally with a 15-minute lifetime. An account is banned and the team wants the user cut off 'immediately'. What is the accurate position?
options: With pure stateless checks the ban takes effect when the token expires (up to 15 minutes); for faster effect add a small denylist or session-version check for sensitive endpoints, and shorten TTLs with refresh tokens
Delete the user's row; the signature will fail
drills.explain: That is the statelessness trade-off. Verification needs no database but cannot see revocations; so revocation needs either a short TTL or some shared state.

drills.q: Forty microservices verify tokens signed with HMAC-SHA256 using one shared secret. A single service is compromised. What is the risk, and the better design?
options: None: only the auth server can create valid tokens
The attacker can mint valid tokens for any user and scope, since verifying and minting use the same secret; use asymmetric signing so verifiers hold only the public key
drills.explain: Symmetric verification means every verifier is also a minter. With a private signing key held by the issuer alone, verifiers can check but never forge.

drills.q: Signing keys rotate: from 12:00 the issuer signs with key B instead of key A. Tokens last 1 hour. Verifiers identify the key by the `kid` header. For how many minutes after 12:00 must verifiers still accept key A?
drills.explain: The last token signed with A was issued just before 12:00 and expires just before 13:00, so A must stay trusted for about 60 minutes. Retire it earlier and valid tokens suddenly fail.

drills.q: Put the stateless verification of a bearer token in order.
items: Parse the token and read its key id (kid) and claims
Fetch (or use a cached copy of) the issuer's public key for that kid
Verify the signature over the payload
Check exp, nbf, issuer and audience
Authorise the request using the scopes in the claims
drills.explain: Authenticity first, then validity, then authority. Never use claims before the signature has been verified.
